params.text:
Welcome

Welcome to this interactive module on Introduction to Research Ethics, developed by the BriGRETE project. This resource is designed for members of Research Ethics Committees (RECs), early-career researchers, and anyone involved in the oversight of research involving human subjects.

Research ethics is a critical foundation for trustworthy science. Throughout this book, you will explore the philosophical roots of ethics, the key international frameworks that guide ethical research, and real-world case studies that test your ability to apply these principles.

params.alt: Slide showing the target audience and learning trajectory for the research ethics module

params.text:
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

  1. Define research ethics and understand the role of ethics in research
  2. Identify the major ethical theories that underpin research conduct
  3. Explain the key international codes and declarations governing research with human subjects
  4. Apply the ALLEA Code of Conduct principles to research scenarios
  5. Analyse case studies involving ethical dilemmas in research
  6. Evaluate the ethical challenges posed by emerging technologies

Navigate through the chapters using the table of contents on the left or the navigation buttons at the bottom of each page. Each chapter contains explanatory text followed by interactive knowledge checks. A comprehensive video lecture is embedded below for those who prefer a multimedia overview.

Estimated Duration: 45 to 60 minutes

The term research ethics (RE) is often used as a synonym for scientific ethics, but it also denotes a narrower field of ethical reflection on scientific research with its specific methods, aims and means and the research process itself. It is very tentative to distinguish this narrower understanding of RE from the broader range of questions of scientific ethics about the relations between science, technology and society, or from those of academic ethics - concerning academic institutions as institutions of knowledge, the values in the life of academic communities, the development of knowledge and its teaching.

RE refers to ethical principles and rules in an internal field of science, but also to ethical considerations related to scientific interventions in the external world - in the research process itself, and in the application of the knowledge, technology or products achieved.

These groups will benefit from tailored, accessible content that enhances their knowledge, compliance practices, and decision-making abilities in research ethics, contributing to a more inclusive and responsible research community.

Research Ethics Committee (REC) Members:

  • Members who review and oversee research projects to ensure ethical standards are met, including new REC members who may benefit from structured, foundational training.
  • Experienced REC members looking to deepen their understanding of specialized topics, such as AI ethics or digital data ethics.

Researchers:

  • Early-career researchers (postgraduate students, PhD candidates, and postdoctoral researchers) who need foundational knowledge in research ethics.
  • Mid-career and senior researchers, especially those engaging with advanced ethical issues in areas like AI, data management, and interdisciplinary research.

The purpose of the module is to introduce the field of research ethics and to present the aims of research ethics training and education. These are related to enhancing awareness of the responsibilities of scientists - in their research activities and to society, to familiarising with good practices in scientific research, ethical principles and rules for responsible behaviour in science, to raising awareness of the ethical challenges associated with the development of modern science and technology.

By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

  • Understand the role of ethics in scientific research and in the scientific community;
  • Recognize the value of freedom of scientific inquiry and independent scientific research against economic, political, and other interests that might affect its objectivity;
  • Know what professionalism and research integrity mean, what knowledge, competences and personal qualities the practice of science implies;
  • Be familiar with the ethical principles in scientific research and the content of ethical concepts that are the basis of moral evaluation of actions and practices - human dignity and freedom, good and duty, benefit and harm, responsibility;
  • Be aware of the scope of ethical concerns today, directed not only at human beings involved in or directly affected by research, but also at animals in research and the environment.

params.text:
Defining Research Ethics

In its narrow definition the research ethics can be defined as a set of ethical principles and rules that guide scientific research practices. It covers primarily issues that concern responsible conduct of research and research integrity, scientific misconduct, protection of human subjects and animals in research, environmental impact of research, etc.

The internal domain of research ethics covers principles that govern scientific practice from within: honesty in reporting results, integrity in methodology, proper attribution of credit, and responsible data management. These norms ensure that the scientific enterprise functions reliably.

The external domain addresses the impact of research on the wider world. This includes the protection of human research subjects, environmental considerations, social responsibilities, and the potential consequences of scientific discoveries on society.

params.text:
• Ethics is a philosophical discipline associated with critical reflection on human actions, on morality as a unique characteristic of the life of the human beings and moral experience.
  • Ethics is the exploration of good life questions in a community - together with others.
  • Theories in ethics explore the nature of human values, ground principles and rules for action, and criteria for judging what is good, right, and just.
  • Adherence to moral principles and rules of conduct is a result of personal choice and conviction. It is the basis for building bonds of trust and meaningful relationships, for cooperating with others.
  • Different theories in ethics set different criteria for assessing actions.

Virtue ethics emphasizes character building and the qualities of character (virtues) that manifest themselves in good deeds and make a person's life good.

Deontological theories focus on the concept of duty and the roots of human obligations.

Utilitarian theories evaluate actions according to the benefit and harm they bring to the person who performs the action and those affected by it.

panels.title: 2. Defining the scope of research ethics

params.text:
Ethics has been associated with reflection on inquiry as a specific human activity and way of life, on methods for achieving true knowledge, since its formation as a philosophical discipline in the 5th-4th centuries BC.

The subject area of a research ethics emerged, however, only at the beginning of the modern era with the development of experimental science and experimental practices in the 17th century, first in physics and then in the life sciences. The study of nature aims to achieve knowledge of nature and the patterns in natural processes that allows predictions to be made and, subsequently, processes to be controlled and driven in a desired direction. The experimental method from the natural sciences becomes the leading model for scientific inquiry. Science enters the world and changes the world, and its slogan, formulated by Francis Bacon, is to achieve a "mastery over nature".

Modern scientific inquiry is tied not only to the pursuit of knowledge, but also to the improvement of human life and to ensuring the prosperity of societies.

The field of medical experimentation on human beings emerged as a field of study fraught with ethical problems in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Systematic reflection on the problems of experimenting on human beings and animals for scientific purposes was developed much later. It was largely prompted by the revelations and published documents on experimental practice during the World War II, but also due to the expansion of experimental activities after the war. The first international regulations in the field were elaborated - the 1947 Nuremberg Code and the 1964 WMA Declaration of Helsinki, last revised in 2024.

In the following decades, the research participant protection mechanisms we are familiar with today were introduced - the requirement for informed consent, the mandatory review of research protocols by IRBs or RECs - not only for their scientific quality, but also with regard to the ethical aspects of research, with special attention paid to protections of vulnerable individuals and groups.

In the 1980s and 1990s, in connection with reports of research fraud and increased cases of misconduct in research practices - the narrower field of research ethics took shape as a territorial ethics of science, with a focus on responsible conduct in research, research integrity and building a culture of integrity in research communities, as well as on learning best practices and preventing misconduct.

params.text:
Why Ethics is Essential to Science

Ethical principles are not externally imposed constraints on research; they are integral to the scientific enterprise itself. The pursuit of true knowledge depends on honesty, accuracy, and reliability within the scientific community. Because science is inherently collaborative, researchers must be able to trust the data and findings shared by their peers.

Adherence to ethical standards serves several vital purposes:

  • Ensuring trustworthy knowledge: The acquisition of genuine knowledge requires that data is collected, analysed, and reported with integrity.
  • Maintaining public trust: Society supports research through funding and participation. Without ethical conduct, public confidence erodes and the social contract between science and society breaks down.
  • Protecting individuals: Ethical standards safeguard the rights, dignity, and welfare of research participants and communities.

During the 1980s and 1990s, reports of fraud and misconduct led the research community to develop a more systematic approach to research integrity, establishing codes of conduct and training programmes to foster a culture of ethical awareness.

• Ethical principles are not externally imposed; they belong to science and are tied to achieving the goal of scientific inquiry - the acquisition of true knowledge. They are the concern and responsibility of the research community itself.
  • Science is a collective endeavour in which the advancement of knowledge takes place through information exchange and communication within the scientific community. Scientific work entails collaboration. Collaboration implies honesty, accuracy, precision, openness, reliability, mutual respect.
  • Researchers are socially responsible - for the research they conduct, the way they conduct it, and the way they present their results.
  • There are areas of particular sensitivity with regard to ethics in science - cases of fraud and misconduct in science, conflicts of interest, abuse or lapses in the protection of human beings, animals, the environment, personal data privacy.
  • Adherence to ethical standards ensures trust among scientists within the scientific community, trust in them within society, and ensures public support for research.

params.text:
Freedom of Scientific Inquiry

Freedom of scientific research is recognised as a fundamental right in many national constitutions and international declarations. This freedom allows researchers to choose their topics, define their goals, develop methodologies, and present findings based on their professional expertise.

However, this freedom is not absolute. It is limited where the protection of research subjects or other serious societal interests are at stake. Conflicts of interest, whether financial, political, or institutional, can compromise the objectivity that society depends upon. The independence of research from external pressures is therefore vital for maintaining impartial, evidence-based contributions to public knowledge.

Research Integrity

Scholars A. Shamoo and D. Resnik identify two senses of research integrity:

  • The rule-following sense: Integrity as compliance with established legal and professional regulations, codes of conduct, and institutional policies.
  • The virtue sense: Integrity as a personal quality characterised by consistency between convictions and actions, intellectual honesty, and a genuine commitment to the values of truthful science.

Professionalism in science combines the mastery of specialised knowledge with conduct that meets the ethical standards of the research community. A culture of integrity requires both individual commitment and supportive institutional environments.

The research is defined as "a systematic investigation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge". It follows established scientific methods and procedures, uses established techniques and tools and achieves knowledge that is verifiable, unbiased and universally valid.

  • Freedom of scientific inquiry is a fundamental value protected as a fundamental human right in international documents and national constitutions. (See: European Commission. European Charter of Researchers, 2005; Art. 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, 2012.) Scientists are free to define the goals, methods and means of their research, and to freely discuss ideas, theses and theories.
  • The independence of scientific research and researchers from economic or political influences is particularly important for the advancement of knowledge, but also for societies in general, in which the objective and impartial presentation of scientific findings as well as the independent judgements of scientists is of particular importance.
  • Freedom of research also has limits - especially where the protection of human beings or animals in experiments, the protection of public goods and serious risks of harm are concerned.
  • As research becomes increasingly commercialised and more closely linked to industry and business, potential conflicts of interest and conflicts of commitment are also becoming more prominent. These need to be addressed in a timely and appropriate manner.

Professionalism is related to the mastery of a body of knowledge, but also to conduct consistent with the ethical requirements of the profession.

The concept of research integrity in a narrow sense is linked to intellectual honesty and the researcher's probity in his/her research activities, in his/her relations with colleagues and all those engaged in research.

In a broader sense, the concept (1) is linked to the knowledge and following of ethical, legal, professional and institutional rules, to principled behaviour and (2) characterizes the overall personality with personal qualities /virtues/ and convictions, consistency in actions and decisions. A. Shamoo and D. Resnik refer to (1) rule-following sense and (2) virtue sense of the concept of integrity. (Shamoo, Resnik. 2015, p. 15)

In recent years, particular attention has been paid to creating an appropriate environment and culture of research integrity, which is tied to long-term and sustained efforts by institutions and their leadership to promote best practices in research, personal and institutional cultures of integrity.

See: Singapore Statement on Research Integrity, 2010. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3954607/

params.text:
The ALLEA Code of Conduct

The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, published by ALLEA (All European Academies), provides a framework for the self-regulation of the research community within the European Research Area. It articulates four key principles:

  • Reliability: Ensuring quality in research design, methodology, analysis, and use of resources.
  • Honesty: Developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting, and communicating research transparently and without bias.
  • Respect: Showing respect for colleagues, research participants, society, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and the environment.
  • Accountability: Taking responsibility for all aspects of the research process, from conception through publication and beyond.

params.alt: Slide defining the FFP spectrum of research misconduct: fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism

params.text:
Research Misconduct: The FFP Spectrum

The most serious forms of research misconduct are collectively known as FFP:

  • Fabrication: Making up results and recording or reporting them as if they were real.
  • Falsification: Manipulating research materials, equipment, or processes, or changing or omitting data so that results are not accurately represented.
  • Plagiarism: Using another person's ideas, words, or intellectual property without appropriate credit.

Beyond FFP, other breaches of responsible conduct include improper citation practices, unnecessary fragmentation of publications (salami slicing), selective reporting of results, and failure to disclose conflicts of interest. Ethics training should promote not only compliance with rules but also the development of ethical awareness and moral reasoning among researchers.

It generally means adherence to established ethical principles and rules of conduct in the scientific community throughout the entire research process - from conception, planning and design, through implementation to publication and dissemination of results.

The Code of Conduct for Research Integrity of the All European Academies (ALLEA), which aims to provide a framework for the self-regulation of the research community in the European Research Area, states that researchers’ expertise in their fields, including their knowledge, methodological skills, and understanding of ethical practices in their respective fields is crucial for research.

Key principles in the document:

  • Reliability in ensuring the quality of research, as reflected in the research design, methodology, analysis, and use of resources.
  • Honesty in developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting, and communicating research in a transparent, fair, complete, and unbiased manner.
  • Respect for colleagues, research participants, research subjects, society, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and the environment.
  • Accountability for the research from idea to publication, for its management and organisation, for training, supervision, and mentoring, and for its wider societal impacts.

See ALLEA, 2023 - https://allea.org/portfolio-item/european-code-of-conduct-2023/

Particularly important in this respect are:

  • the introduction of mandatory training in research ethics;
  • responsible scientific mentoring;
  • the development of guidelines and institutional procedures for investigating and addressing research misconduct, and their clear articulation in codes and regulations.

In the field of science and scientific research, fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism (FFP) are generally considered among the most serious forms of research misconduct. Currently, the laws of most developed countries have definitions of these violations and provide for a legal sanction for misconduct. (See the definitions in ALLEA, 2023 - https://allea.org/portfolio-item/european-code-of-conduct-2023/)

Other breaches concern authorship, co-authorship, and the recognition of research contributions, compliance with intellectual property requirements, incorrect citation, duplication or unnecessary fragmentation of publications.

Violations are usually defined as significant deviations from established research practices in the scientific community, as well as from ethical principles and rules set out in codes of ethics or other documents - institutional, national and international - that address responsible research conduct and research integrity. Such deviations can be found in a wide range of scientific activities, from the preparation and planning of research, the conduct of relevant research procedures, the protection of the research subjects, the organisation of collaborative work, data collection, storage and management practices, to the publication and dissemination of results, peer review, evaluation and editing, as well as the training, guidance, and mentoring of early-career researchers.

params.text:
A History of Protecting Research Participants

The protection of human subjects in research has evolved through a series of landmark international documents, each responding to specific historical events and ethical failures. Together, these documents form the foundation of modern research ethics governance.

params.alt: Slide describing the Nuremberg Code and the Declaration of Helsinki as foundational directives
Slide covering the Belmont Report and CIOMS Guidelines for protecting vulnerable populations

params.text:
The field of medical experimentation on human beings has been crucial in shaping the scope of a research ethic in the years since the World War II. It is in the spotlight not only because the interventions directly affect the lives and health of those involved in experiments, but also because of the instances of malpractice in which the humane nature of medicine is put into question.

The principles of a research ethic are first formulated with respect to medical experimentation, medical and health-related research, and the established criteria for assessing actions and practices are transferable and applicable to other areas of science and research.

This is also the area for which the most detailed guidelines and directives, regulations and international documents have been developed.

The Nuremberg Code is part of the final judgment delivered in August 1947 at the end of the Doctors Trials (1946-1947) in the German town Nuremberg. The trials were against the Nazi doctors who carried out experiments in the concentration camps during the Second World War.

The Nuremberg Code consists of ten principles designed to protect the rights and welfare of research subjects.

The Code begins with: "The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential."

The Nuremberg Code was the first internationally agreed guideline on research involving people.

Read the Nuremberg Code (BMJ)

The Declaration of Helsinki is the most widely known and influential guideline in medical research. It is the official policy of WMA initially promulgated in 1964. It has been revised many times, most recently in 2024.

WMA Declaration of Helsinki

The primary purpose of research:

"The primary purpose of medical research involving human participants is to generate knowledge to understand the causes, development and effects of diseases; improve preventive, diagnostic and therapeutic interventions; and ultimately to advance individual and public health.

These purposes can never take precedence over the rights and interests of individual research participants."

The protection of research participants:

"It is the duty of physicians who are involved in medical research to protect the life, health, dignity, integrity, autonomy, privacy, and confidentiality of personal information of research participants. The responsibility for the protection of research participants must always rest with physicians or other researchers and never with the research participants, even though they have given consent."

Three basic considerations: scientific validity, benefits from research and the risk of harm, ethics and adequate forms of protection for research participants:

"Medical research involving human participants must have a scientifically sound and rigorous design and execution that are likely to produce reliable, valid, and valuable knowledge and avoid research waste. The research must conform to generally accepted scientific principles, be based on a thorough knowledge of the scientific literature, other relevant sources of information, and adequate laboratory and, as appropriate, animal experimentation. The welfare of animals used for research must be respected.

The design and performance of all medical research involving human participants must be clearly described and justified in a research protocol. The protocol should contain a statement of the ethical considerations involved and should indicate how the principles in this Declaration have been addressed. The protocol should include information regarding aims, methods, anticipated benefits and potential risks and burdens, qualifications of the researcher, sources of funding, any potential conflicts of interest, provisions to protect privacy and confidentiality, incentives for participants, provisions for treating and/or compensating participants who are harmed as a consequence of participation, and any other relevant aspects of the research. In clinical trials, the protocol must also describe any post-trial provisions.

The protocol must be submitted for consideration, comment, guidance, and approval to the concerned research ethics committee before the research begins…"

The National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. The Belmont Report. Ethical Principles and Guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research. 1979.

http://ohsr.od.nih.gov/guidelines/belmont.html

The National Commission was established in 1974 by the U.S. Congress with a charge to identify ethical principles and develop guidelines to govern the conduct of research involving humans.

The National Commission sets forth three basic ethical principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

The Commission insisted that these principles require special levels of protection to vulnerable and disadvantageous groups: children, mentally ill, incompetent adults, pregnant woman, and prisoners.

The scientific and ethical aspects of research protocol should be assessed by Institutional Review Boards (IRBs).

The central concern was to ensure that the interests of society, or the enthusiasm of the researcher, do not override the interests of the individual.

The principle of respect for persons gives rise to the moral requirements to obtain informed consent from research subjects and to protect the confidentiality of private information.

The principle of beneficence requires that researchers do not harm and, when possible, promote the welfare of research subjects.

The principle of justice requires fair distribution of benefits and burdens of research.

params.text:
Beyond the Laboratory

The responsibilities of researchers extend well beyond the laboratory and the publication of results. As professionals with specialised knowledge and competence, scientists bear a heightened obligation toward both individual welfare and the broader social good.

Key social responsibilities include:

  • Expert testimony: Providing honest, evidence-based input to policy discussions and legal proceedings.
  • Public communication: Informing the public about research findings, their implications, and their limitations in accessible and transparent ways.
  • Risk warning: Alerting society to potential technological dangers and environmental threats arising from scientific work.
  • Environmental stewardship: Recognising and addressing the ecological impact of research activities and technological development.

The growing complexity of modern science means that researchers increasingly need to consider the societal context and consequences of their work, contributing to informed public debate and responsible innovation.

• Scientists have obligations and responsibilities not only in their scientific work but also towards their colleagues and those involved in or affected by research.
  • Their high level of expertise also entails greater responsibility. Scientists' responsibilities are expanding along with the reach of the technologies they develop and their effects on individual and social life, other living beings, and the environment, including the risks they may pose to life on Earth.
  • Social science research addressing social problems - including those arising from scientific and technological development - has a clear social commitment. Research in the humanities is also highly relevant that explores the changes in our self-understanding as a result of the technologies that are entering our lives.
  • Scientists have an important role to play in informing the public, presenting significant research findings and participating in educational initiatives. In many cases, leading scientists provide warnings about the dangers posed by certain technologies or the risks of their misuse.
  • Scientists have more specific responsibilities in relation to expert testimony in court trials, expert participation on committees to develop guidelines, regulations or policies, or by taking informed positions in public debates.

params.text:
New Frontiers, New Dilemmas

Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, genomics, neuroscience, and synthetic biology are creating ethical challenges that existing frameworks were not designed to address. The convergence of these technologies amplifies their transformative effects, making consequences harder to predict and potentially irreversible.

Key concerns include:

  • Algorithmic bias and AI decision-making: Automated systems can perpetuate or amplify existing inequalities if not carefully designed and monitored.
  • Genetic modification: Technologies such as CRISPR raise fundamental questions about the boundaries of human intervention in biological systems.
  • Dual-use potential: Research intended for beneficial purposes may also be misused for harmful ends, requiring careful risk assessment.
  • Data privacy: Large-scale data collection and analysis challenge traditional notions of consent and confidentiality.

The precautionary principle suggests that when scientific activities raise threats of harm, precautionary measures should be taken even if some cause-and-effect relationships are not yet fully established. This principle is especially relevant in fields where the pace of technological development outstrips our capacity for ethical and regulatory oversight.

Knowledge Check 3

Assess your understanding of the social responsibilities of researchers and the ethical challenges posed by emerging technologies.

The technologies developed in recent decades have enormous transformative potential for humans and human societies. Developments in the fields of AI, genetics and genomics, synthetic biology, neuroscience are largely due to the convergence of technologies, which further amplifies their effects. Technology is transforming all spheres of life, as for example digital technologies are transforming work, education, individual and social life, and global economy.

The so-called emerging technologies have enormous potential for innovation and profit, they are bound to bring unquestioned benefits but also new threats and risks. Assessing them is very difficult in view of the uncertainty about their far-reaching consequences and their irreversibility for humans, living organisms and the environment.

The development of these technologies implies transparency and objective assessment of the effects on human life and health as well as on social life, concern for the public good and balance in policy decisions, legal regulations and control measures, new institutions to initiate discussion and seek solutions on a planetary scale.

The concern in recent years has also been triggered by the awareness of the scale of the ecological crisis, biodiversity loss and climate change. Thus, the challenge is whether humans on a planetary scale will be able to harness the technological power they have acquired and to regulate, manage and appropriately control the technologies they have developed.

The concern with science and new technologies is to ensure that science serves humane purposes, contributes to preserving the conditions for meaningful human life on earth and ensures sustainable development. See: UN, The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development - https://sdgs.un.org/goals

params.text:
Testing Frameworks Against Reality

The true measure of ethical competence is the ability to apply principles to complex, real-world situations. The following case studies present scenarios drawn from actual research contexts. Each case involves ethical dilemmas that require you to draw upon the frameworks and principles covered in earlier chapters.

params.alt: Case File 01: The Falsified Curve depicting a case of suspected data falsification in research
Case File 02: Drug-Free Schizophrenia Research depicting ethical concerns in psychiatric research
Case File 03: Dual-Use H1N1 Reconstruction depicting biosafety and dual-use research concerns

params.text:
Knowledge Check 4

Apply your understanding of ethical frameworks to the case studies you have just reviewed.

panels.title: Case 1: Falsification of Data? — Case Description

params.text:
"You are a graduate student in pharmacology at a large university working under the direction of a senior researcher. After reading a paper on a new serotonin reuptake inhibitor published by the researcher, you notice that there is a problem with a diagram representing the dose-response curve. You cannot reconcile the diagram with the published data. You are a co-author on the paper with a postdoctoral fellow, a technician, and your senior researcher (your supervisor). You approach your supervisor with this problem, and he shrugs it off, saying that you do not understand the research well enough to make a judgment about it. What should you do?"

Source: Shamoo/Resnik, 2015, p. 2

Ethical Issues - research misconduct, collegiality, responsible research mentoring, Whistleblowing/reporting

In many cases of data falsification, a member of the project or research team finds a discrepancy between the data documented in a study and the published data findings.

Falsification of data is among the most serious violations in the sphere of scientific research. It compromises scientific research that aims to achieve certain new knowledge, follows a particular scientific methodology and is grounded in evidence. Such a violation has severe consequences not only for the person who committed it, but for the entire team.

In All European Academies (ALLEA) Code of Conduct from 2023 "Falsification is manipulating research materials, equipment, images, or processes, or altering, omitting, or suppressing data or results without justification".

Depending on the seriousness of the violation, different sanctions may be imposed by governmental control bodies, scientific institutions, funding institutions or journals in which the relevant articles are published.

panels.title: Case 1: Collegial Relations and Responsible Mentoring

params.text:
Collegial relations: The codes of ethics pay special attention to accuracy, honesty, and openness as professional qualities that are particularly important in research as a collaborative enterprise.

Responsible mentoring: Research mentors have a key role and responsibility in providing scientific guidance and promoting research integrity and responsible conduct of research.

The majority of codes, guidelines and instructions state that scientists are obliged to report violations of the good practices of research. Before reporting, the persons reporting must ensure that a violation has occurred and be able to provide evidence sufficient for the case to be further investigated by the appropriate authorities, committees, etc. Failure to report a violation is often interpreted as misconduct and complicity - with the mere awareness of a violation. On the other hand, however, to raise an allegation without evidence could be qualified as bad faith reporting.

Often, reporting cases of misconduct has negative effects on the reporting persons, especially those who are at the beginning of their scientific career. They may be forced to start at another university/research institution, start their research over again, or suffer from the reputation gained as a whistleblower.

The reporting persons must first make sure that the discrepancy they have discovered is actually present. It is advisable further for the student to have conversations with the team members to clarify the situation. It should be borne in mind that for there to be a violation the falsification must have been deliberately committed. In many cases, discrepancies are due to errors or deficiencies in research documentation. Researchers need to maintain confidentiality in these conversations, as hasty disclosure of an unconfirmed misconduct may irreversibly and undeservedly damage the researcher's credibility.

Attention should also be paid to the fact that each of the co-authors in a research publication is responsible not only for the part of the work he or she has done, but also for the content of the entire publication. The text should be accessible to all co-authors and reviewed before it is submitted for publication.

References: Shamoo, A.D., Resnik, D.B. Responsible Conduct of Research. Oxford, New York: Oxford University Press, Third edition, 2015. | All European Academies (ALLEA) The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity. Revised Edition, 2023. ALLEA | International Committee of Medical Journals Editors. Recommendation for the Conduct, Reporting, Editing, and Publication of Scholarly Work in Medical Journals. Updated January 2024. ICMJE | The Embassy of Good Science - Misconduct & Misbehaviors

panels.title: Case 2: Drug-Free Research with Mentally Ill — Case Description

params.text:
In the study the University of California at Los Angelis (UCLA) Medical School the participants - patients with schizophrenia, were included first in a one-year, fixed-dose study in which they received the antipsychotic drug Prolixin decanoate. On the completion of the first-year study, subjects who gave their consent were enrolled in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Some of them were assigned to receive the same dose of Prolixin, others to receive a placebo injection. The study presupposes the cross-over of the groups after twelve weeks. Subjects who were still stable after an additional twelve weeks period were assign to a withdrawal protocol, or to stop their medication for at least one year, if no relapse or some other exacerbation occurs. One patient from those enrolled in the withdrawal protocol committed suicide after completion of the one-year drug withdrawal study, another one experienced a severe psychotic relapse. The lawsuit was filed against UCLA by the family of one of the subjects. The federal Office of Protection from Research Risks (OPRR) issued a report on its investigation of complaints.

Ethical issues - Drug-free research in schizophrenia, the level of risk in research with vulnerable individuals, decision-making capacities and informed consent, the use of placebo

We may ask: If there is a standard treatment that alleviates the symptoms and reduces the acute psychotic episodes (even if not efficient in all cases and with substantial side-effects), what justifies the withdrawal of this standard care for patients with schizophrenia from their own physicians involved in this case also as investigators?

If we think about the significant risks of relapse for the participants in the drug-free research but nevertheless we accept the importance of the study we should ask further questions: was the design of the study appropriate and what safeguards were envisaged for reducing the risk and assuring the adequate forms of consent?

panels.title: Case 2: Level of Risk, Vulnerable Individuals, Decision-Making Capacity

params.text:
The level of risk: The crucial questions concern also the level of acceptable risk and the measures undertaken for protecting participants and reducing of risks. The study of UCLA presupposes one year without antipsychotic medications - the risks for the patients were predictable according to the available statistic data. The patients who received placebo were exposed to significant risk related not only to the possible worsening of their health condition, but risk for their relationships and their lives.

Vulnerable individuals: The mentally ill are considered vulnerable group in research primarily because of their limited or lacking decision-making capacity. The group of the mentally ill is however a diverse group of individuals including seriously retarded individuals who have never been fully competent, senile individuals who were ones competent but are no longer competent, and psychiatric patients who may alter the condition and also the level of competence. There are different regulations and provisions relevant to their involvement in research. See the WMA Declaration of Helsinki (Art. 19 and 20).

Decision-making capacity: The patients with schizophrenia may have a fluctuating capacity. In this case they were considered competent to give consent for the participation in the study and no additional measures for measuring their decision-making capacity were included in the protocol.

According the WMA Declaration of Helsinki:

"The benefits, risks, burdens, and effectiveness of a new intervention must be tested against those of the best proven intervention(s), except in the following circumstances:

If no proven intervention exists, the use of placebo, or no intervention, is acceptable; or

If for compelling and scientifically sound methodological reasons the use of any intervention other than the best proven one(s), the use of placebo, or no intervention is necessary to determine the efficacy or safety of an intervention; and the participants who receive any intervention other than the best proven one(s), placebo, or no intervention will not be subject to additional risks of serious or irreversible harm as a result of not receiving the best proven intervention. Extreme care must be taken to avoid abuse of this option."

Questions: Do you have any ethical concerns with this proposed study? Should the study include a placebo group? A washout period? Do you have any suggestions for improving the study?

The study of UCLA raises general questions concerning the research with mentally ill patients (in this case - patients with schizophrenia): questions related to the special risks and the mechanisms of reducing them as well as to the assessment of competence and the adequate informed consent procedures. The study raises also specific questions that concern the use of placebo and the justification of the drug-free trials with patients with schizophrenia.

The goal of the study was to identify predictors of successful functioning of patients without psychotic medications. The identification of good predictors could spare the negative effects of the currently available antipsychotic medication for some patients. The study of the pathophysiology of schizophrenia may also "lead to the development of more specific, effective, and safer forms of treatment". These seems to be important goals that could justified the drug-free research.

If we consider the nature of the disease, the possible fluctuations in decision-making capacity, the treatment resistant behaviour of patients with schizophrenia, and their need of support we should think also for the forms of adequate protection (adequate tests for the assessment of competence, consent monitoring process, and even re-consenting process combined with surrogate consent).

In the study of UCLA there were also problems with the withdrawal of consent - the boy who experienced the relapse and his patient reported that their appeals to the research team were neglected and it took nine months before the boy was put back on medication.

In the discussions following the UCLA study diverse opinions were expressed - among them positions for the ban of all studies involving prolonged drug-free periods.

Note: The case description is based on Appelbaum, P.S. "Drug-Free Research in Schizophrenia: An Overview of a Controversy" IRB, 1996, Volume 18 Number 1:1-5.

References: WMA Declaration of Helsinki - WMA | UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, 2006. UN CRPD

The term was introduced at the beginning of the 21st century to refer to research that may be used for either good or bad purposes. The recent controversies concerned above all experiments with dangerous pathogens and toxins.

WHO definition of dual-use research of concern from 2020: WHO DURC

"Dual-use research of concern (DURC) describes research that is intended to provide a clear benefit, but which could easily be misapplied to do harm. It usually refers to work in the life sciences, but the principles are also applicable to other fields including engineering and information technology. It encompasses everything from information to specific products that have the potential to create negative consequences for health and safety, agriculture, the environment or national security."

The ethical issues raised by such research affect scientists, funding institutions, scientific journals, and society. Typically, significant benefits are expected from this type of research, but there are also serious security and safety concerns.

International organisations and governments are setting up special committees to develop recommendations on how to proceed with this type of research and its results, and policies to reduce the risk of experimentation.

This can be achieved by various interventions - e.g. modification of protocols to reduce the risks of accidental contamination or misuse of results, regular verification of experiments, review/verification of evidence for medical countermeasures for agents and toxins, treatments and vaccines. If this is not sufficient, funding may be cut off and the study denied, or in view of the results, key information may be revised for publication and communication or the study classified. Some journals introduce additional review of dual-use research texts submitted for publication.

Much research related to new technologies developed in recent years has been associated with possible dual use - gene editing, synthetic biology, etc.

In 2005, Tumpey and associates published a paper in Science describing the reconstruction of the H1N1-Virus that in 1918 caused the so-called Spanish flu. The material for the reconstruction was extracted from victims of the virus frozen in the Alaskan ice. One of the scientists was involved in the sequencing of the virus genome and the reconstruction was undertaken before the sequencing was published in 2005. In the following years, the scientists conducted studies comparing the lethality of the virus with other viruses in studies with mice, they also investigated what proteins through what mechanisms are responsible for virulence.

panels.title: Case 3: Ethical Issues — Freedom, Risk, Biosafety, Responsibility, Biosecurity

params.text:
Research freedom: While freedom of scientific inquiry is considered a fundamental right, it could be limited and must be balanced if in conflict with other rights or values - such as public safety. Research has undoubted benefits related to medical knowledge about the virus, but there are also concerns that a newly synthesised virus could be a powerful weapon in the hands of terrorists, for example.

Risk assessment: To justify such a study, it is necessary to show that the benefits outweigh the risks of the study. The problem in such cases is that the risks are difficult to assess or there is uncertainty about the risks.

Biosafety: Fears of an accidental security breach, in which the virus could infect a researcher or be released from the lab, also seem reasonable. WHO 2024, p. XIII - Definition: "Biosafety. Containment principles, technologies and practices that are implemented to prevent unintentional exposure to biological agents or their inadvertent release."

Moral responsibility of scientists and others: Such research raises questions about how far the responsibility of scientists extends, what are the responsibilities of the state in funding such research, of the companies or institutions involved in DNA synthesis, and of the editors of scientific journals that publish the results of research.

Biosecurity: WHO 2024, p. XIII - Definition: "Biosecurity. Policies, principles, technologies and practices implemented for the protection and control of and accountability for biological material, technology and information or the equipment, methods, skills and data related to their handling. Biosecurity aims to prevent intentional or accidental unauthorized access to, and loss, theft, misuse, diversion or release or even weaponization of such commodities."

The benefits of the study are not only related to information about the virus causing the disease. Using the reconstructed virus, its pathogenicity was investigated. According to the scientists the knowledge gained would allow adequate measures when a new virus with similar characteristics emerges and also the development of vaccines and therapies.

Scientists say that in this case the dangers were not so high because they were working in a laboratory with high biosecurity standards where the risk of spread of the virus outside the laboratory was minimal. They also claim that the virus is not as dangerous today because effective antiviral treatments are available.

A vaccine has been developed in mouse experiments and shown to be effective in preclinical trials. Also in mice, a vaccine developed against Swine Flu in 2009 was found to be effective against Spanish Flu.

With regard to risk, the precautionary principle should be borne in mind. Various formulations of it are known, but in general, when there is a threat to public health and safety, scientists are required to develop, implement and follow special precautions.

In many cases, scientists alert themselves to dangers, and they are obliged to do so when certain research poses excessive risks. An example is the 1975 Asilomar Conference, at which leading scientists in the field of recombinant DNA discussed the risks and also the necessary regulations in the field.

Note: The case description is based on Deplazes-Zemp, A. Ethik in der Biotechnologie. In: Elger, B., Biller-Andorno, N., Rutsche, B. (Hrsg.) Ethik und Recht in der Medizin und Biowissenschaften. 2014, S. 170-177.

References: Deplazes-Zemp, A. Ethik in der biotechnologie. In: Elger, B., Biller-Andorno, N., Rutsche, B. (Hrsg.) Ethik und Recht in der Medizin und Biowissenschaften. Walter de Gruyter, Berlin/Boston, 2014. | Tumpey T.M. et al., Characterization of the reconstructed 1918 Spanish Influenza pandemic virus. Science 2005, 310: 77-80. | World Health Organization, 2024. Laboratory biosecurity guidance | National Institute of Health, Dual-Use research

params.text:
Summary

Throughout this module, you have explored the fundamental principles, historical milestones, and contemporary challenges of research ethics. Here are the key takeaways:
Ethical principles are not external constraints but belong to science itself. Honesty, accuracy, and reliability are prerequisites for the collective pursuit of knowledge.

The Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki, the Belmont Report, and the CIOMS Guidelines form the backbone of human subjects protection. The ALLEA Code provides a comprehensive framework for research integrity in Europe.
Research integrity involves both following established rules and cultivating personal virtues such as intellectual honesty, consistency, and moral courage.
Fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism are the most serious offences in research. A culture of integrity, supported by training and institutional mechanisms, is essential for prevention.
The convergence of AI, genomics, and other technologies creates ethical challenges that require proactive, interdisciplinary approaches and the application of the precautionary principle.
Scientists have a duty to communicate honestly with the public, provide expert input to policy, and consider the broader societal impact of their work.

Next Steps

This module has provided a foundation in research ethics. As you continue your work in research or on a Research Ethics Committee, remember that ethical awareness is not a one-time achievement but an ongoing commitment. Stay informed about evolving standards, engage in continued training, and contribute to building a culture of integrity in your institution and community.

Thank you for completing this module. We wish you well in your ethical research journey.
